headline: El Nino forecast poses potential drought risk to Australian wine growing regions but conditions remain wet on the ground
reasoning: El Nino is forecast for the Australian summer, raising concerns about agricultural volatility and drought risk for wine grape growing regions like Mildura and the Riverland. However, conditions on the ground remain very wet with more rainfall than seen in recent years. El Nino can bring extremes of both wet and dry conditions. The company is proactively locking in water and managing varietal renovation to transition red grape supply to white, though this takes multiple years to bear fruit.
quote: Agriculturally there's always a risk when you think about drought we're not seeing it convert on the ground yet. It's still incredibly wet. Mildura or the Riverland has had more rain than they've seen in a number of years. And that's El Nino. It comes with kind of highs in both wet and dry. So we are forecasting or everyone is foreseeing a potential dry spell that will come not seeing it yet. Um, locking in water, making sure that we're prudent about our water use around our varietal or renovation turnover because we still want to change red supply into white, but it takes multi-year to come to fruition.

headline: Australian Vintage's McGuigan zero-alcohol wine is growing double-digit but off a very small base, while McGuigan core is under pressure in the UK due to tax-driven price inflation.
reasoning: Zero-alcohol wine continues to grow double digit for Australian Vintage, driven by 'zebra stripe' consumption where consumers alternate between alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages. However, zero-alcohol remains a single-digit share of the total alcohol market, so the main game is still conventional wine. McGuigan core has declined in the UK partly due to government-led tax changes pushing up prices across the industry, while holding flat in Australia — where heavy reds under $10 have seen the largest decline — is viewed as a relative share gain. The UK market requires further work.
quote: The pleasing thing about our zero is it continues to grow double digit. It's showing a consumer demand for that kind of product more now evolved into what's called zebra stripe consumption. You'll have an alcoholic beverage and you'll follow up by a zero alcoholic beverage. And so people tend to opt in to less consumption. But offsetting it with that, McGuigan core has declined in the UK, but holding it flat in Australia is actually a good result because, like I said, heavy Reds sub $10, which is where we over index has seen the larger proportion of decline.

headline: Australian Vintage CEO says turnaround is working after returning to positive free cash flow in FY26 for first time since FY22.
reasoning: CEO Tom Dusseldorp confirmed the turnaround is on track after taking the role 12 months ago. The company returned to positive underlying free cash flow of $2 million in FY26, cut net debt to $89 million, and revenue edged up to $258 million. The focus was on fixing cash working capital by aligning supply to shifting consumer demand and exiting two vineyard assets (Balranald and Mullewa). The company says it is now in balance from vintage 27 and plans to pay down net debt by a further $13–$14 million in FY27.
quote: Yeah I can safely say it is. I think taking the role 12 months ago, there was quite a bit of clarity needed for the organisation to unlock. What we saw was growth savings and ultimately a path to profitability over time. But we had to get the baseline cash movement right, and we've proven that we can do that.

headline: All major wine companies are suffering a multi-year demand shift away from heavy reds toward lighter, brighter varietals and lower-alcohol options.
reasoning: Post-Covid, the wine industry benefited from elevated revenues and suppressed costs, which masked an emerging consumer trend toward lighter wines — rosés, whites, and sparkling — while heavy reds began to decline. This shift is slow to correct because supply is tied to long-lead agricultural growers. Younger consumers are drinking less per occasion, favouring convenience formats and smaller purchases rather than bulk buying at large-format liquor stores. Wine has been perceived as a high-ABV, rack-and-save category, which limits its versatility for dip-in, dip-out consumption occasions.
quote: Post Covid, everyone in liquor had a phenomenal couple of years where they had great revenues growing and really no costs. It kind of masked what was emerging as a future trend of health a need for lighter, brighter varietals, rosés, white, sparkling and heavy reds just started to turn. And so that's really what has exposed Australian vintage. All the major wine companies are suffering that shift in demand, which takes multi-year to mop up because it is linked to growers and agricultural supply.

headline: Australian Vintage plans no further acquisitions in FY27, focusing instead on consolidating Mad Fish investment and paying down net debt by $13–14 million.
reasoning: Having invested in the Mad Fish brand in the first half of last year, management's FY27 priority is to consolidate that acquisition rather than pursue further strategic deals. The company intends to pay down net debt this financial year, which would represent an additional $13–$14 million improvement in cash on a like-for-like basis — taking the cumulative improvement to nearly $50 million.
quote: So no other acquisitions plan. We did that investment in the first half of last year. Our cash flow was positive, excluding investments. So some investors were like, you know, what is the plan for 27? It's actually to consolidate those investments, not to make any more strategic kind of acquisitions. We plan to pay our net debt down this financial year, FY 27. So on a like for like basis, regardless of what cash moves through the business, that'll be another 13 to $14 million improvement on cash.
episode_title: Australian Vintage raises a glass to a turnaround
